title: Rules of the Conversation
blurb: Talk about conversation norms in different cultures

steps.html:
How close you stand, how long you stay silent, how loudly you speak — none of it is universal. This lesson looks at what changes across cultures, and at the questions you use to find out.

  • Talk about conversation norms in different cultures
  • Ask subject, object and indirect questions accurately
  • Listen to a talk for gist and for detail

steps.title: You are going to hear a talk on cross-cultural communication.
steps.sub: Which of these do you expect it to say changes most between cultures?

steps.title: Listen to the opening. What is the speaker's main point?
options: Some languages are much harder to learn than others.
Understanding the words is only part of successful communication.
Most misunderstandings between cultures are caused by poor grammar.
steps.answer: Understanding the words is only part of successful communication.
steps.why: She opens by saying communication involves far more than simply understanding each other's words.

steps.title: Listen again. Which three things does she say we need to be aware of?
options: Vocabulary, grammar and how strong your accent sounds to other people
Distance, acceptable topics, and whether it is all right to interrupt or be silent
Somebody's age, their income, and which way they vote
steps.answer: Distance, acceptable topics, and whether it is all right to interrupt or be silent
steps.why: She lists how far apart we stand, which topics are acceptable, and whether it is OK to interrupt or to be silent.

steps.title: Listen again. What happens if you stand too far away?
options: People think you are being respectful.
You give the impression of being distant and unfriendly.
People assume you have not understood them.
steps.answer: You give the impression of being distant and unfriendly.
steps.why: Too close makes people feel awkward; too far away gives the impression of being distant and unfriendly.

steps.title: Listen. True or false?
steps.prompt: Most Europeans and North Americans are comfortable with long silences.
steps.why: She says most Europeans and North Americans avoid long silences.

steps.title: Listen. True or false?
steps.prompt: For many Europeans, a silence can suggest that you are not interested in the topic.
steps.why: Silence is read as something negative: uncomfortable, shy, angry, or not interested.

steps.title: Listen. True or false?
steps.prompt: In some East Asian countries, silence is understood as a sign of respect.
steps.why: She says silence is seen as a positive thing — it shows respect and shows you are listening.

steps.title: Listen. Why does she mention Brazil?
options: Because Brazilians rarely disagree in public.
Because an enthusiastic Brazilian discussion can sound to others like an argument.
Because Brazilians speak more softly than northern Europeans.
steps.answer: Because an enthusiastic Brazilian discussion can sound to others like an argument.
steps.why: People from South America and southern Europe tend to speak more loudly, so an enthusiastic discussion can be mistaken for a row.

steps.title: The speaker asks: How far apart do you stand during conversation?
options: Because the question word asks about the subject of the verb.
Because the question word asks about something other than the subject, so the auxiliary is required.
Because the verb is in the present perfect.
steps.answer: Because the question word asks about something other than the subject, so the auxiliary is required.
steps.why: How far apart is not the subject — you is. Questions that ask about anything except the subject need an auxiliary. This is the rule you will study next.

steps.title: Read between the lines.
steps.sub: The speaker says that in Brazil an enthusiastic discussion can sound like an argument to outsiders.
steps.prompt: Why does she choose that example rather than simply saying 'volume varies between cultures'?
options: Because Brazil is the country where people speak most loudly.
Because it shows the practical cost of the difference: the listener draws a wrong conclusion about the mood.
Because she has spent time in Brazil and is drawing on her own experience.
steps.answer: Because it shows the practical cost of the difference: the listener draws a wrong conclusion about the mood.
steps.why: Her whole talk is about misreadings, not about the differences themselves. The example is chosen because it produces one.

steps.title: Language noticing.
steps.sub: She calls silence in a conversation 'comfortable' in some cultures and 'awkward' in others, rather than 'normal' and 'strange'.
steps.prompt: What does that choice of words tell you about her position?
options: She thinks one of the two is correct and the other is a mistake.
She is describing how the silence feels to the people in it, not judging which practice is right.
She is being vague because the research is unclear.
steps.answer: She is describing how the silence feels to the people in it, not judging which practice is right.
steps.why: Comfortable and awkward both describe an experience. Normal and strange would make one of them the standard.

steps.title: Subject questions and object questions
steps.html:
Read the rule, then study the examples. The practice comes after.

Most questions in English need an auxiliary verb — do, does, did, have, is, will — placed before the subject: Who did she interrupt?

But when the question word (who, what, which, how many) is the subject of the verb, there is no auxiliary and no inversion. The word order is the same as a statement: Who interrupted her?

Compare the two. In Who did she interrupt? the answer is the person who received the action. In Who interrupted her? the answer is the person who did it.

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Subject questions on the left of each pair, object questions on the right.

Who made that gesture?
Subject question — no auxiliary. Answer: Ben made it.

Who did Ben make that gesture to?
Object question — did + subject + verb.

What causes most misunderstandings?
Subject question — what is doing the causing.

What does she find awkward?
Object question — she is the subject.

How many people attended the meeting?
Subject question — the number is the subject.

How many people did you invite?
Object question — you is the subject.

Which topic offended him?
Subject question.

Which topic did he raise?
Object question.

Who is dominating the conversation?
Subject question with be — still no extra auxiliary.

Who are they talking to?
Object question; the preposition stays at the end.

What happened at lunch?
Subject question. Not What did happen at lunch?

Who told you that?
Subject question. Not Who did tell you that?

steps.title: From statement to question
steps.html:
Turning a statement into both kinds of question.

  1. Start with the statement: Her manager offended Marta at lunch.
  2. To ask about her manager — the subject — replace it with who and change nothing else: Who offended Marta at lunch?
  3. To ask about Marta — the object — replace her with who, then add the auxiliary and put the subject back: Who did her manager offend at lunch?
  4. Check: the subject question has no did. The object question has did and the main verb returns to its base form (offend, not offended).

steps.title: Softer, more careful questions
steps.html:
An indirect question begins with a polite opening — Could you tell me…, Do you know…, I was wondering… — and then continues in statement order.

Inside an indirect question there is no inversion and no do / does / did: Could you tell me where the meeting is? — not where is the meeting.

If the direct question has no question word, use if or whether: Do you know whether he is coming?

The final punctuation follows the opening: Could you tell me…? is a question, but I was wondering… and I'd like to know… take a full stop.

steps.title: Example bank.
steps.html:
Notice that a subject question keeps its shape inside an indirect question — there was never an auxiliary to remove.

Could you tell me how far apart people stand here?
Statement order after the opening.

Do you know what the safest topics are?
what are the safest topics is wrong here.

I was wondering whether you had a row.
No question word, so whether.

Could you tell me if this gesture causes offence?
If and whether are both fine.

Do you know who made the complaint?
Subject question — unchanged inside the indirect form.

I'd like to know why she interrupted me.
Full stop, because I'd like to know is a statement.

Do you happen to know when the meeting finishes?
when does the meeting finish is wrong here.

Could you tell me how long you have been working here?
Present perfect continuous keeps statement order too.

steps.title: You are going to write a short guide for a visitor to your country.
steps.sub: Which three of these will you cover? Choose three.

steps.title: Write the guide.
steps.sub: 120–150 words. Use at least four words or phrases from this lesson and at least two questions.
steps.html:
• Open by naming your country and the situation.
  • Cover your three areas, one short paragraph each.
  • Include at least one subject question and one indirect question.
  • Close with the single piece of advice you would give first.

Useful language

  • In my country, people usually stand about … apart.
  • It is normal / unusual / considered rude to …
  • If you …, you might make someone feel awkward.
  • A safer topic would be …
  • Visitors often ask why we … / whether it is acceptable to …
  • Could you tell me …? / Do you know whether …?
steps.modelHtml:
Conversation in Kazakhstan — a short guide

People here stand fairly close, about forty centimetres apart, and standing further away can make you seem cold rather than polite. Silence in the middle of a conversation is not a problem, so you do not need to fill every pause.

The safest topics with someone you have just met are food, family and the weather. Asking about salary is common between colleagues, but a visitor who asks it in the first meeting may put their foot in it.

Two questions visitors often ask me are Who normally pays in a restaurant? and Could you tell me whether it is rude to interrupt? The answer to the second is that a short interruption to agree is welcome; a long one is not.
